messages.subject: Re: [stan] Feature/fix ldlt (#419)
parts:
Let me start by saying that it's great people are volunteering
to contribute code at all. I really appreciate what Marcus is
doing to help.

I'm sympathetic to both sides of this discussion.

I'm not convinced we need to test every private helper function
we use. I'd rather put energy into properly specifying and
testing the higher-level functions that are actually exposed.

Also, if we start enforcing rules at the syntactic level like every
function needs a test, our developers, being good problem solvers,
might start wiggling around the intent by cutting-and-pasting code into
monolithic functions to cut down on unit-testing requirements.

At the same time, I'm fully behind the practice of writing code
modularly enough that functions can be documented and hence
tested. Documentability is a precondition for testability, because
we need to understand the intent of a function to test it.

These particular functions are important and complicated, so it's perhaps
not surprising they're causing some level of frustration with
testing and integration. I think part of the problem is that neither
Daniel nor I are comfortable enough with all of these matrix operations
to understand what's intended by looking at the code; this is why we're
worried about maintainability.

A middle ground would be to add some doc on what they're supposed
to do and how to test them. I'm willing to help write the tests if
I can understand what they're supposed to be.

I'm probably the most guilty of all of us by not unit testing and
documenting the parser. I really do hope to shore it up after 2.1.0 is
out, but other more pressing issues keep coming up. The lack of testing
is what's blocking some changes to the parser I'd like to make and
also blocking Robert Goedman's pull request for C++11 compatibility.
So I feel Marcus's frustration firsthand as well.

- Bob


On 12/19/13, 10:45 PM, Daniel Lee wrote:
> @mbrubake, I understand your distinction between public API vs private API,
> but that isn't a reason to not test something.
>
> I'm asking to add unit tests to LDLT_alloc for a few reasons:
> - it's hard to instantiate. Having a unit test showing the next developer
> how to instantiate it would cut down hours of work just figuring out how to
> call it directly.
> - it does a lot of work. Lots of things depend on it. I would feel much
> more comfortable if it was tested.
> - if I'm looking at just the class, how am I to know what compute() or
> log_abs_det() do, what the valid values of its arguments are, and if it is
> even safe to call?
>
> My motivation for having tests in is to save time for the next person that
> has to touch the code. If existed an example test that instantiated the
> class in a standalone test that, in and of itself, saves a lot of time.
> Knowing how to call each of the functions saves a whole lot more. Given
> that the class isn't well documented (and I'm not asking you to document
> it), the minimal amount of courtesy you can provide to the next person that
> has to look at this code is to provide some documentation on how to use it
> and a little bit of code that shows that it doesn't crash.
>
> If you're having trouble creating tests, then there's a problem with the
> design of the code. If you're not creating unit tests out of principle,
> someone else will need to write tests before the pull request gets in.
>
> It'll take you a lot less time to write 3 tests (one for the constructor,
> one for compute(), one for log_abs_det()), than it will take for anyone
> else to write those three tests. I've already sunk a lot of time into
> breaking everything apart and testing the rest of the untested,
> undocumented functions, so please return the courtesy and write 3 tests.
>
>
>
